title: A complete Citroën 2CV4: the useful inventory of the cabin and the parts still present
author: codex-blog-rewrite
excerpt: On a complete 2CV4, the cabin, seats, controls and small parts quickly reveal whether the car was stripped or left waiting. A detailed inventory starts before dismantling.
content:
When a complete 2CV4 reaches the workshop, the first useful job is not to take everything apart at once. The cabin, controls and small parts still tell an important story. On our Doubs car, the interior had remained in place. That alone changes the value of the base, because it avoids having to reconstruct later what could be noted, photographed and preserved on the first day.

The cabin tells you whether the car was stripped

On a 2CV, the driving area speaks quickly: steering wheel, pedals, speedometer, levers, seats, simple trim, handles and the condition of the mountings. A car left open for years or used as a donor shows it immediately. By contrast, an interior that is still present gives a sound starting point for inventory and later reassembly.

In the case of this 2CV4, the cabin was not fresh, but it was readable. That makes it possible to photograph the controls before removal, identify the small parts that are still there and prepare a clean dismantling sequence instead of rebuilding everything from memory months later.

Photograph before you remove

The most profitable reflex is often the camera. Before removing a seat, a switch or a loom section, record screw positions, cable routes, trim placement and the state of the fixings. On a simple car like the 2CV, those details look trivial until the day comes to put them back.

This image work is not decorative. It prevents improvised assembly, forgotten spacers and pointless repeat dismantling. A useful inventory starts with concrete reference points taken while the car is still complete.

Spot what can truly be kept

An inventory is not only a list of missing parts. It is also a way to save what deserves to remain. An original rear bench, a complete set of controls, a period-correct speedometer or specific hardware can save time and keep the project honest.

At the same time, parts that are still present must not be accepted automatically as good. A hardened seal, a tired cable or a bent fixing should be classed as items to inspect, not as validated parts. A useful inventory separates those two situations clearly.

Small parts often speak loudest

On a 2CV4, small parts often tell more than the major assemblies: handles, knobs, hinges, brackets, lids, screws, covers and cable passages. When those details are still there, the car was often left waiting rather than broken up in haste. That nuance matters when deciding the time and budget of the whole project.

The page devoted to this 2CV4 from the Doubs puts this inventory back into its buying context. For the structural and mechanical side, the natural next step is the 2CV4 restoration page.
